response.title: Is a used or refurbished power station worth buying, and how do I tell how much battery life is left?
response.answer:
Yes, a used or refurbished portable power station can be a great deal, especially if it uses a LiFePO4 (LFP) battery. But the key is understanding how much battery capacity remains, not just whether the unit powers on.

A power station can display 100% charge while having lost 20–30% of its original battery capacity.

These are broad ranges, not guarantees. Actual lifespan depends on temperature, charging habits, discharge depth, and battery management.

A three-year-old LiFePO4 power station that has been used occasionally might still have over 90% of its original capacity. Conversely, a heavily used unit could be significantly degraded.

The most useful metric is State of Health (SOH), which measures remaining capacity relative to the original capacity.

markup:
**Yes, a used or refurbished portable power station can be a great deal**, especially if it uses a LiFePO4 (LFP) battery. But the key is understanding how much battery capacity remains, not just whether the unit powers on.

A power station can display 100% charge while having lost 20–30% of its original battery capacity.

## 1. Is buying used or refurbished worth it?

| Condition | My recommendation |
|---|---|
| Manufacturer refurbished, with warranty | <badge color="success">Best option</badge> |
| Used LiFePO4, tested, good discount | Good value |
| Used NMC lithium-ion, unknown history | Higher risk |
| Won't charge to 100%, shuts off unexpectedly | Avoid |
| Swollen, damaged, or recalled battery | Avoid |

The battery chemistry makes a major difference.

| Battery type | Typical advertised cycle life to 80% capacity |
|---|---|
| LiFePO4 (LFP) | 2,500–4,000+ cycles |
| NMC lithium-ion | 500–1,000 cycles |

These are broad ranges, not guarantees. Actual lifespan depends on temperature, charging habits, discharge depth, and battery management.

A three-year-old LiFePO4 power station that has been used occasionally might still have over 90% of its original capacity. Conversely, a heavily used unit could be significantly degraded.

## 2. How to measure remaining battery life

The most useful metric is **State of Health (SOH)**, which measures remaining capacity relative to the original capacity.

\[
SOH=\frac{\text{Current battery capacity}}{\text{Original battery capacity}}\times100\%
\]

For example, suppose you're buying a 1,024 Wh power station.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text color="secondary" weight="medium" size="xs">EXAMPLE BATTERY HEALTH</text>
  <row align="baseline" gap={2}>
    <title size="2xl" color="default" tabularNums>85%</title>
    <text color="secondary" size="sm">remaining capacity</text>
  </row>
  <box background="surface-tertiary" height="12px" radius="full" clip>
    <box background="rgba(38,150,100,0.9)" width="85%" height="100%" radius="full"/>
  </box>
  <row justify="between">
    <text size="xs" color="secondary">0 Wh</text>
    <text size="xs" color="secondary">1,024 Wh original</text>
  </row>
  <text weight="medium">870 Wh remaining</text>
  <text color="secondary" size="sm">Approximately 154 Wh of capacity has been lost.</text>
</box>

The challenge is that many power stations do not display battery SOH directly. Fortunately, you can estimate it through a controlled discharge test.

### Method A: Use a watt-hour meter (most practical)

<AsyncImageGroup query={["P3 Kill A Watt electricity usage monitor plug in watt hour meter","portable LiFePO4 power station with AC power meter and lamp plugged in"]} aspectRatio="5:4" shop_eligible={true}/>

1. Charge the power station to 100%.
2. Disconnect all charging inputs.
3. Plug an AC watt-hour meter (such as a Kill A Watt) into the power station.
4. Connect a steady 100–200W load, within the station's rated output.
5. Run it until the station reaches its normal low-battery cutoff.
6. Record the total energy delivered in Wh or kWh.

For a 1,024 Wh station, suppose you measure 740 Wh at the AC outlet.

You cannot directly call that 72% battery health because the inverter consumes energy too.

If you assume 85% AC efficiency:

\[
SOH \approx \frac{740}{1024\times0.85}=85\%
\]

That is an **estimated** SOH, not a definitive measurement. Actual inverter efficiency varies by model and load. Comparing your result with a new unit of the same model under identical conditions is more reliable. <Cite refs={["turn849622search10","turn849622search3"]}/>

### Method B: Check the manufacturer's app

Some models or diagnostic systems expose battery cycle count, SOH, or other battery data. Others show only charge percentage.

Ask the seller for a screenshot of the battery information, if available. A cycle count is helpful, but it doesn't reveal the complete battery condition.

## 3. How much should you pay?

These are my suggested buying thresholds, not current market price averages.

| Condition | Maximum I'd consider paying vs. new |
|---|---:|
| Manufacturer refurbished, warranty | 70–80% |
| Used LFP, tested, excellent condition | 60–70% |
| Used LFP, unknown battery health | 40–50% |
| Older NMC, unknown history | Under 40% or skip |

Compare against the **current discounted new price**, not the original MSRP. Also verify that any warranty actually transfers to you.

## 4. Battery health and value calculator

{@body const soh = valid ? out/(cap*eff/100)*100 : 0}
